correctness.rationale: For distinct binary four-mers, endpoints determine every possible greedy overlap (length at most 3). The exact F recurrence minimizes savings over every maximizing ordered pair; the Held–Karp D recurrence computes the true shortest superstring. An integer-arithmetic C++17 exhaustive scan of all 65535 nonempty subsets gives sharp maximum 17/11 and four masks. A separate literal-string witness checker verifies each chosen merge is globally maximal and that the eight-word optimum is 11 by checking every 8! source ordering. Finite arguments prove only the specified finite domain.

originality.rationale: The examined primary papers cover unrestricted-alphabet bounds for word lengths three, four, and at least ten, but none computes a fixed binary four-mer exact ratio or its complete maximizing orbit. Mathematical research-index searches and accessible historical source/claim/parameter comparisons found no covering equivalent; a distinct prior binary length-three census is non-implicative. Historical priority outside indexed and inspected records remains uncertain.
residual_risks: An unindexed equivalent binary four-mer enumeration may exist.
The 2018 paper was assessed only through its official abstract; no full-text NOT_COVERING claim is made about it.
The finite exhaustive checker is not an independently audited external certificate.

value.rationale: At fixed binary alphabet and word length four, this is a natural complete problem domain (all sixteen edges of the order-three binary de Bruijn graph and all 65535 input sets), not a selective example. The sharp approximation constant, complete four-extremizer orbit, and handling of every adversarial greedy tie give a reproducible benchmark that differs sharply from unrestricted-alphabet four-mer lower bounds and from the binary three-mer situation. No extension to arbitrary word length is claimed.
